title: An Unstructured Supplementary Service Data System for Daily Tracking of Patient Samples and Diagnostic Results in a Diagnostic Network in Malawi: System Development and Field Trial (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Diagnostics in many low- and middle-income countries are conducted through centralized laboratory networks. Samples are collected from patients at remote point-of-care health facilities, and diagnostic tests are performed at centralized laboratories. Sample transportation systems that deliver diagnostic samples and test results are crucial for timely diagnosis and treatment in such diagnostic networks. However, they often lack the timely and accurate data (eg, the quantity and location of samples prepared for collection) required for efficient operation. OBJECTIVE This study aims to demonstrate the feasibility, adoption, and accuracy of a distributed data collection system that leverages basic mobile phone technology to gather reports on the quantity and location of patient samples and test results prepared for delivery in the diagnostic network of Malawi. METHODS We designed a system that leverages unstructured supplementary service data (USSD) technology to enable health workers to submit daily reports describing the quantity of transportation-ready diagnostic samples and test results at specific health care facilities, free of charge with any mobile phone, and aggregate these data for sample transportation administrators. We then conducted a year-long field trial of this system in 51 health facilities serving 3 districts in Malawi. Between July 2019 and July 2020, the participants submitted daily reports containing the number of patient samples or test results designated for viral load, early infant diagnosis, and tuberculosis testing at each facility. We monitored daily participation and compared the submitted USSD reports with program data to assess system feasibility, adoption, and accuracy. RESULTS The participating facilities submitted 37,771 reports over the duration of the field trial. Daily facility participation increased from an average of 50% (26/51) in the first 2 weeks of the trial to approximately 80% (41/51) by the midpoint of the trial and remained at or above 80% (41/51) until the conclusion of the trial. On average, more than 80% of the reports submitted by a facility for a specific type of sample matched the actual number of patient samples collected from that facility by a courier. CONCLUSIONS Our findings suggest that a USSD-based system is a feasible, adoptable, and accurate solution to the challenges of untimely, inaccurate, or incomplete data in diagnostic networks. Certain design characteristics of our system, such as the use of USSD, and implementation characteristics, such as the supportive role of the field team, were necessary to ensure high participation and accuracy rates without any explicit financial incentives.

summary.oneLiner: A basic-phone USSD reporting system gave Malawi's diagnostic network daily sample data; a field trial suggests it is feasible, adoptable and accurate.
summary.overview: Many low- and middle-income countries send patient samples from remote clinics to central labs, but the transport system often lacks timely data on how many samples are ready for pickup. The authors built a text-menu system (USSD, a simple messaging channel that works on any basic mobile phone) that lets health workers submit daily counts of ready samples and results at no cost. They ran it for a year across 51 health facilities in three Malawian districts. The paper suggests the system was feasible, adopted by most facilities, and accurate, without any financial incentives.
summary.question: Can a distributed data collection system built on basic mobile phones (USSD) reliably gather daily reports on the number and location of patient samples and test results ready for transport in Malawi's diagnostic network?
summary.method: The authors designed a USSD-based reporting system and ran a year-long field trial. Health workers submitted daily reports of sample and result counts, and the authors monitored daily participation and compared the submitted reports with program data to assess feasibility, adoption and accuracy.
summary.data: 51 health facilities serving 3 districts in Malawi, with daily reports from July 2019 to July 2020; the facilities submitted 37,771 reports. Accuracy was checked against the number of patient samples a courier actually collected from each facility.
findings: Daily facility participation rose from an average of 50% (26/51) in the first 2 weeks to about 80% (41/51) by the trial's midpoint, and stayed at or above 80% until the end.
On average, more than 80% of a facility's reports for a given sample type matched the number of samples a courier collected from that facility.
The authors suggest a USSD-based system is a feasible, adoptable and accurate solution to untimely, inaccurate or incomplete data in diagnostic networks.
The authors state that the use of USSD and the supportive role of the field team were necessary for high participation and accuracy without explicit financial incentives.
summary.whyItMatters: The paper suggests that low-cost phone-based reporting can give sample transport administrators the timely, accurate data they need to run collection and delivery efficiently in centralized diagnostic networks. The authors point to the design choice of USSD and the support provided by field teams as key to high participation without paying facilities.
